newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - Romania selloff on track, but outcome uncertain.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Romania selloff on track, but outcome uncertain.

text.p: Romania's largely successful mass privatisation programme, timed carefully with Sunday's presidential and parliamentary elections in mind, has been one of the few bright spots on the country's bleak financial horizon.
Prime Minister Nicolae Vacaroiu's government has been criticised for being slow off the mark with the year-old plan.
But the scheme, among the most ambitious in eastern Europe, has worked, though the final outcome is still uncertain.
"Like it or not, the Vacaroiu government stayed on track and managed to complete the free transfer of property to private hands," said independent analyst Ilie Serbanescu.
"The move was clever," added another analyst. "Bringing the scheme nearer to the polls has earned them political capital."
The programme gave all Romanians over 18 non-transferable coupons entitling them to acquire shares in the state firm of their choice.
Fifteen million of 17 million potential shareholders took up the offer -- a far cry from an earlier issue of vouchers which most hard-pressed consumers sold quickly to bring in a handful of dollars.

For most Romanians, swapping the coupons for up to a 60 percent stake in 4,000 companies was a shot in the dark. The government offered little economic data on the mass selloff of companies, many of which had made no profit in years.
About 1,800 companies were even oversubscribed. A further 1,000 hit or nearly hit the 60 percent mark.
"These companies are no longer majority state owned," said Iacob Zelenco, presdient of the National Privatisation Agency (ANP).
The remaining 40 percent is earmarked for cash sales to local and foreign investors.
NO PROBLEM ATTRACTING BUYERS
Analysts expect little difficulty in attracting buyers for clothing firms, hotels, wine producers or breweries. Firms in oversized sectors will almost certainly take longer to sell.
The ANP, together with the State Ownership Fund (FPS), handles privatisation in Romania, was founded in 1992 as part of the country's moves to a market economy.
"Considering the FPS's selloffs so far the number of privatisations in Romania is quite substantial," Zelenco said.
Romania's privatisation schemes differed from those in other post-communist countries by involving direct swaps to individuals without the intervention of investment funds.
A separate FPS scheme privatised a further 2,600 firms through worker-management buyouts, direct sales and auctions.
The way forward is not so clear.
The government's critics say little has been done to restructure bloated industry -- as sought by the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank to secure further credits.
"Romania now has to complete true privatisation, the sale of 40 percent, which is the rougher part," Serbanescu said.
Romania's industry, he said, tends to be lacking in specialisation and should be re-equipped and restructured to make factories attractive to domestic and foreign investors.
Restructuring is also essential to rejuvenate exports, down 10 percent in the first eight months of the year.
"An oversized sector such as steel should be partly closed down. We continue to make raw steel when we need special steels, which we import," Serbanescu said.
"Restructuring is needed even if the social costs are high. Other countries did this even though it hurt them. Romania does not have to invent the wheel all over again."
Western analysts agree.
"No investor will want to buy a whole construction materials company. He will be more interested in taking over its brick factory," one analyst told Reuters.

"And there is the issue of redefining prices of industrial assets. Nobody will pay big money for empty or rusty halls. But restructuring needs time, probably 15 years, and allowing prices to drift is not something you can achieve overnight."
State corporate shares in Romania have a face value of around 25,000 lei ($7.41) -- viewed as artificially high -- and this is the minimal price at which they have been sold so far.
"With such problems solved, foreign investors will not hesitate to come. And there will be plenty of domestic investors interested in acquisitions using banking credits," said a local economist.
Officials say Romania needs legislation to ease cash sales to foreign portfolio investors.
Present rules do not cover portfolio investors, who have to undergo the same intricate procedures followed by direct investors. Red tape can delay some transactions by four months.
Foreign investment remains thin in Romania, with just over $2.0 billion pumped in since the 1989 end of communism, compared with $11 billion in Hungary and $10 billion in Poland. ($1=3375 Lei)
